Business Understanding¶

  • The goal of this project is to understand what affects salaries in data-science jobs and to see if we can predict a job’s salary in USD. We look at factors like where the company is located, the type of job, experience level, employment type, work setting, and company size.

  • Our main question is, that we want to answer, is: “Can we predict a data-science salary using job's/ company's features in the provided dataset?”

  • This is useful because it helps job seekers know what they can expect to earn, and it helps companies make fair and competitive salary decisions.

Variable Selection and Creation¶

# Step 2: Drop variables not useful for modeling 
data.drop(['salary_currency', 'job_title', 'salary', 'employee_residence'], axis=1, inplace=True)

# Step 3: Construct New Variables

# make 'company_location' categorical with top 6 locations, rest as 'Other'
top_6 = data['company_location'].value_counts().nlargest(6).index

data['company_location'] = np.where(data['company_location'].isin(top_6),
                                    data['company_location'],
                                    'Other')

# Convert all categorical columns to numeric codes
categorical_cols = ['company_location', 'job_category', 'experience_level', 
                    'employment_type', 'work_setting', 'company_size']

for col in categorical_cols:
    data[col + '_code'] = data[col].astype('category').cat.codes

# drop original categorical columns
data_numeric = data.drop(columns=categorical_cols)

# Check result

Step 2: Regression Modelling - Model Selection using Linear Regression based on training set¶

Using a stepwise approach - we will use a stepwise forward approach first and then a backwards one and pick the best model if different.

Stepwise Forward¶

To do this you start by trying all the variables singly and picking the best model. Then repeat the process until there is no improvement. Each model is evaluated based on its R Squared Adjusted value which is generally between 0 and 1 with a higher value being better. The R-Squared Adjusted value is based on the RMSE value (calculated as the square root of the mean squared error)

TLDR: You build a model with 1 variable at a time. Adding 1 variable to the model each time until the Rsq Adj shows no improvement

In [ ]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

# List of possible predictor variables (candidates)
# These are all variables we are willing to test in the model.
# Forward selection will choose from this list one at a time.
candidateVariables = [
    'work_year',
    'company_location_code',
    'job_category_code',
    'experience_level_code',
    'employment_type_code',
    'work_setting_code',
    'company_size_code'
]

# Start with no variables selected.
# Forward selection adds variables step-by-step.
modelVariables = []

# This will hold the best model at the end.
best_model = None

# Forward Selection Loop
# Runs as long as there are still unused candidate variables.
while candidateVariables:
    
    # Store adjusted R^2 values when each candidate variable is added.
    adj_r2_with_candidates = {}
    
    # Try adding each remaining candidate variable individually
    # to the current model, then record its adjusted R^2.
    for var in candidateVariables:
        temp_model = sm.OLS(
            y_train,
            sm.add_constant(x_train[modelVariables + [var]])
        ).fit()
        
        # Store adjusted R^2 for this candidate
        adj_r2_with_candidates[var] = temp_model.rsquared_adj

    # Select the variable that produced the highest adjusted R^2
    best_var = max(adj_r2_with_candidates, key=adj_r2_with_candidates.get)
    best_candidate_r2 = adj_r2_with_candidates[best_var]

    # Add the first variable automatically if none selected yet,
    # or add it if it improves the model.
    if not modelVariables or best_candidate_r2 > best_model.rsquared_adj:
        
        # Add the variable permanently to the model
        modelVariables.append(best_var)
        
        # Remove from the candidate list (cannot select it again)
        candidateVariables.remove(best_var)
        
        # Fit an updated model using all selected variables
        best_model = sm.OLS(
            y_train,
            sm.add_constant(x_train[modelVariables])
        ).fit()
        
        # Print step-by-step progress
        print(f"Added {best_var}, AdjR2 = {best_model.rsquared_adj}")
    
    else:
        # No improvement -> Stop the forward selection        
        break
    
print("\nFinal Model Variables:")
modelVariables

print("\nFinal Model Summary:")
best_model.summary()

Stepwise Backwards¶

To do this you start by taking the model with all variables and removing variables singly and checking which variable improves the model the most. Then repeat the process until there is no improvement. Each model is evaluated based on its R Squared Adjusted value which is generally between 0 and 1 with a higher value being better. The R-Squared Adjusted value is based on the RMSE value (calculated as the square root of the mean squared error)

TLDR: Opposite of forwards. instead of building up you put all variables into the model and remove variables until the Rsq Adj is lower than the prev

In [ ]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

# Start with all predictor variables
# Backward elimination removes the weakest ones step-by-step
# based on adjusted R^2
modelVariables = [
    'work_year',
    'company_location_code',
    'job_category_code',
    'experience_level_code',
    'employment_type_code',
    'work_setting_code',
    'company_size_code'
]

# Loop until removing a variable would decrease adjusted R^2
while True:
    # Store adjusted R^2 when each variable is removed
    adj_r2_without_var = {}

    # Try removing each variable individually
    for var in modelVariables:
        temp_model = sm.OLS(
            y_train,
            sm.add_constant(x_train[[v for v in modelVariables if v != var]])
        ).fit()
        adj_r2_without_var[var] = temp_model.rsquared_adj                       

    # Find the variable whose removal gives the highest Adj R^2
    worst_var = max(adj_r2_without_var, key=adj_r2_without_var.get)
    best_adj_r2_after_removal = adj_r2_without_var[worst_var]

    # Fit the current model to get current adjusted R^2
    current_model = sm.OLS(
        y_train,
        sm.add_constant(x_train[modelVariables])
    ).fit()
    current_adj_r2 = current_model.rsquared_adj

    # If removing the variable improves Adj R^2 -> remove it
    # Otherwise -> stop
    if best_adj_r2_after_removal > current_adj_r2:
        print(f"Removing {worst_var} improves AdjR^2 from {current_adj_r2:.4f} to {best_adj_r2_after_removal:.4f}")
        modelVariables.remove(worst_var)
    else:
        print("\nAll remaining variables are improving or stable in Adj R^2.")
        break

# Final model after backward elimination
final_model = sm.OLS(y_train, sm.add_constant(x_train[modelVariables])).fit()

print("\nFinal Model Variables:")
modelVariables

print("\nFinal Model Summary:")
final_model.summary()

Removing employment_type_code improves AdjR^2 from 0.2107 to 0.2108

Compare the Stepwise Forward and Stepwise Back Models¶

In [ ]:
# Stepwise Forward and Backward Model Comparison

# Forward Selection Result
forward_optimal_vars = ['job_category_code', 'experience_level_code', 
                        'company_location_code', 'work_year', 
                        'company_size_code', 'work_setting_code']
forward_adj_r2 = 0.2108  # Adjusted R^2 from forward selection model

print("Forward Selection Model:")
print(f"Optimal Variables: {forward_optimal_vars}")
print(f"Adjusted R^2: {forward_adj_r2:.4f}\n")

# Backward Elimination Result

backward_optimal_vars = ['work_year', 'company_location_code', 
                         'job_category_code', 'experience_level_code', 
                         'company_size_code']
backward_adj_r2 = 0.2110  # Adjusted R^2 from backward elimination model

print("Backward Elimination Model:")
print(f"Optimal Variables: {backward_optimal_vars}")
print(f"Adjusted R^2: {backward_adj_r2:.4f}\n")

# Comparison and Recommendation

print("Comparison:")
if backward_adj_r2 > forward_adj_r2:
    print("Backward Elimination is slightly better based on Adjusted R^2 and statistical significance of predictors.")
else:
    print("Forward Selection is slightly better based on Adjusted R^2.")

Model Comparison Conclusion¶

Backward Elimination is the better model.

  • Reasons:

    • Same adjusted R^2 (no loss in predictive power)

    • Uses fewer predictors (5 instead of 6)

    • All remaining predictors are statistically significant

    • More parsimonious and less prone to overfitting

    • Produces a cleaner, more interpretable regression model

Step 3: Regression Modelling - Model Evaluation based on the TEST set¶

In [ ]:
# Evaluate the final model on the TEST set
# Summary Measures: MAE, MAPE, RMSE
import numpy as np

# Add constant to test set for prediction
x_test_evaluate = sm.add_constant(x_test[['work_year', 'company_location_code', 
                                          'job_category_code', 'experience_level_code', 
                                          'company_size_code']])

# Predict salaries on the test set
ypred_test = modelFinal.predict(x_test_evaluate)

# Calculate error metrics

# Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
Prediction_test_MAE = np.mean(np.abs(ypred_test - y_test))

# Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
Prediction_test_MAPE = np.mean(np.abs((ypred_test - y_test) / y_test)) * 100 # % form

# Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
Prediction_test_RMSE = np.sqrt(np.mean((ypred_test - y_test) ** 2))

# Print the results
print(f"MAE: {Prediction_test_MAE:.2f} USD")        # Average absolute error
print(f"MAPE: {Prediction_test_MAPE:.2f}%")         # Average percentage error
print(f"RMSE: {Prediction_test_RMSE:.2f} USD")      # Root mean squared error

Findings¶

Main Results and Conclusions.¶

Univariate Analysis¶

  • work_year - Majority of data lies between the 2022.5 - 2023 range, by a considerable amount too. Any data before the year 2023 are considered outliers

  • salary - Majority of data lies between the 100,000 - 200,000 range, with a dramatic dropoff when salary starts going over that range. Data over the 300,000 range are outliers and there are quite a few of them

  • salary_in_usd - Exact same information as salary, only difference is currency. Numbers are very similar as most of the salaries recorded are from the US

  • job_category - Most abundant category is is “Data Science and Research”, with “Data Engineering” not too far behind. Too little data in “Cloud and Databases” for it to even matter

  • salary_currency - Proves point made for salary_in_usd. The large majority of salary recorded is in USD. The rest are way too small to worry about

  • experience_level - Most of the data recorded has experience of a senior. Entry levels and executives are almost tied with each other

  • employment_type - Like salary_currency, an overwhelming amount of data is going into one type, and that is “Full-time”

  • work_setting - Data is not too erratic here. Most is going to “In person”. “Remote” is half of that, while “Hybrid” is very last

  • company_size - A large amount of the comapnies are of M (medium) size. S (small) companies are the least frequent ones

Bivariate Analysis¶

  • salary_in_usd vs. company_size - Median salary is highest for Large (L) and Medium (M) companies, which are very similar with each other (around USD 140K). Small (S) companies have the lowest median (around USD 75K).

  • salary_in_usd vs. job_category - Salaries in Machine Learning and AI, Data Science and Research, and Data Engineering/Architecture have the highest median/upper quartile (around USD 180K to USD 200K). Data Quality and Operations, and Data Management and Strategy have the lowest median (around USD 100K).

  • salary_in_usd vs. experience_level - Executive-level roles show the highest median salary (around USD 180K). Senior and Mid-level are next, with very similar medians (around USD 150K). Entry-level has the lowest median (around USD 75K).

  • salary_in_usd vs. work_setting - In-person and Remote work settings have very similar median salaries (around USD 150K). Hybrid work has the lowest median salary (around USD 80K). Another cool thing to note, is that the maximum salary before outliers is also lowest for Hybrid work.

Multivariate Analysis¶

  • salary_in_usd vs. work_year - Salary distribution increases from 2020 to 2023, with the majority of data points and highest salaries occurring in 2023. High salary outliers are present across all years.

  • _salary_in_usd vs. salary_in_usd - Many data points fall on the diagonal, meaning the local salary equals the salary_in_usd . Other points below the diagonal show where large local currency salaries are converted into much smaller salary_in_usd values.

Decision Tree Modelling¶

  • After training a Decision Tree Regressor to predict salaries, the model was able to capture some patterns in the data but had limited accuracy. Using an 80/20 train-test split gave us enough data to train the model, and the decision tree mainly split on features like experience level, job category, and company location.

  • However, the performance scores show that the model is only moderately effective. The average error (MAE) is about USD 39,000, and the RMSE is about USD 51,000, which means many predictions are far from the true salary. The R² score of 0.31 indicates that the model explains only 31% of the salary differences in the dataset.

  • Overall, the results suggest that salary depends on more detailed information than the fields we currently have from the Kaggle dataset, and that a single decision tree may not be strong enough to capture all the complexity. More advanced models that we have not learnt yet will definitely improve prediction accuracy.

Feature Engineering¶

Data Cleaning:¶
- The dataset contained no missing values, so no imputation was required.
Variable Reduction:¶
- Removed variables that were not useful for prediction or duplicated information:
- These included: salary_currency, job_title, salary, employee_residence.
Categorical Consolidation:¶
- company_location was simplified by grouping all but the top 6 most frequent locations into an “Other” category. Reduced noise and improved model .generalization.
Encoding:¶
  • All remaining categorical variables were converted to numeric category codes for modelling:
    • company_location_code
    • job_category_code
    • experience_level_code
    • employment_type_code
    • work_setting_code
    • company_size_code
Final Feature Set for Modelling:¶
- After preprocessing, the dataset contained a clean, numeric set of predictors suitable for regression analysis and machine learning.
Conclusion:¶
- Feature engineering successfully transformed complex raw categorical data into a structured, modelling-ready format while reducing dimensionality and preventing overfitting.

Regression Modelling¶

Stepwise Linear Regression (Forward vs Backward):¶

  • Both forward and backward stepwise selection were performed to identify the most significant predictors. Backward Elimination Selected the Best Model.

  • Final variables selected (all statistically significant, p < 0.05):

    • work_year
    • company_location_code
    • job_category_code
    • experience_level_code
    • company_size_code

  • Removed due to insignificance:

    • employment_type_code
    • work_setting_code
Model Performance:¶

  • Adjusted R^2 ≈ 0.211 for both forward and backward models

  • Backward was preferred because It used fewer predictors

  • All included predictors were statistically significant

Test Set Evaluation¶

  • Using the final backward-elimination model:

    • MAE: ~ (39,011)

    • MAPE: ~ (31%)

    • RMSE: ~ (51,379)

    • This indicates moderate accuracy. The model captures general salary trends but cannot fully predict individual salaries due to unobserved factors (e.g., skills, negotiation, industry).

Highlight key visualizations that support findings.¶

Feature Engineering¶

Histograms & Boxplots of Numeric Variables:¶

  • Salary and salary_in_usd showed strong right-skew and high outliers.

  • Boxplots across categories (experience, job type) revealed wide salary dispersion.

  • Insight: Confirmed salary variability and justified simplifying categories and expectations of moderate predictive accuracy.

Bar Charts of Categorical Variables:¶

  • Displayed dominant classes (e.g., full-time jobs, U.S. locations, senior workers).

  • Insight: Supported encoding decisions and highlighted imbalance in several predictors.

Regression Modelling¶

Correlation Heatmap¶

  • Identified moderate relationships between salary and experience, job category, company size, and location.

  • Insight: Guided variable selection for regression.

Salary vs Categorical Boxplots¶

  • Clear median salary differences across job category, experience level, and company size.

  • Insight: Reinforced inclusion of these variables in final regression model.

Predicted vs Actual Scatterplot¶

  • Wide dispersion around the diagonal line.

  • Insight: Model captures direction/trends but not exact salary values.

Residual Error Plots¶

  • Residuals centered around zero but with high variance.

  • Insight: Model is unbiased but limited by missing explanatory factors.
